newsitem.title: USA: Toyota tries to block Republic purchase.
newsitem.headline: Toyota tries to block Republic purchase.

text.p: Toyota Motor Corp. on Wednesday asked the Texas Motor Vehicle Board to halt the sale of a Toyota dealership to Republic Industries Inc., making it the first major automaker to mount a legal challenge to Wayne Huizenga's fast-growing megadealer empire.

Toyota's Toyota Motor Sales U.S.A. unit argued in its petition the proposed purchase of Joe Myers Toyota in Houston would harm the public interest and threaten the Japanese automaker's marketplace representation.

Toyota said Republic is violating the company's standard dealer agreement of waiting nine months in between dealership purchases. In February, Republic bought Kendall Toyota and Kendall Lexus, both in Florida. Lexus is Toyota's luxury division.

Republic has refused to sign the agreement for the Joe Myers dealership, and told Toyota it wants to eventually buy 59 Toyota dealerships over the next 18 months -- representing about 20 percent of its annual Toyota brand sales.

"To be honest with you, they've not operated a new car dealer for more than four or five months. How can we turn over up to 20 percent of our volume to an unproven entity?" said Jim Press, general manager of the Lexus division, as well as a board member and senior vice president for Toyota Motor Sales U.S.A.

Toyota currently limits one owner to seven Toyota division dealerships nationally, and has a formula for restricting common ownership in a given sales region. For Lexus, the company limits owners to three dealerships on a national basis, and two in a region.
The company has had previous informal guidelines for dealership transactions, but only formalized them within the last year, said Press.

Republic, the Fort Lauderdale, Fla.-based parent company for the AutoNation dealership chain, has been on a buying binge since December 1996, and is now the country's largest auto retail chain. Industry trade magazine Automotive News estimated that as of March 17 Republic had 90 franchises with $4.3 billion in 1996 revenues.

Republic spokesman Ron Castell declined to comment on the petition because he said the company had not seen it. He said Republic has reached umbrella agreements with several other automakers, including General Motors Corp., Ford Motor Co. and Chrysler Corp..
"We've had great relations with most of them and we assume we'll have great relations with the others," he said.
However, automakers have been slow to embrace publicly traded dealerships and the burgeoning superstore concept, fearful of losing their long-held power over the dealer body.

Ford, for example, has imposed limits on publicly traded dealerships that are different from traditional arrangements. GM's Saturn Corp. has refused to approve franchise agreements with Republic -- even though the dealers themselves have signed sale agreements.

Donald Keithley, who oversees dealer relations for industry consultant J.D. Power and Associates, said Toyota is nevertheless taking a risk by opposing AutoNation because consumers may find they like the store's concept.
"I would guess their position a year from now would be different from what it is today," he said.
